articles.title: How to make your science business succeed when you’re a female founder
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01904-ySexist assumptions and a male-dominated culture can make it harder for women to attract investment for the companies they set up.
articles.content:
Emma Yates, chief scientific officer at Proteotype Diagnostics, would like to see more funding and support for founders during parental leave. Credit: Wesley Sukdao, Proteotype CEO

An estimated 25 million women across the world’s most advanced economies are being denied the opportunity to launch and develop their own businesses, and those who do typically have more-modest growth ambitions than male founders, finds a report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)1.

According to the Bridging the Finance Gap for Women Entrepreneurs report, published at the end of last year, the gender gap in start-up financing is particularly stark in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) sectors. The OECD trawled studies from 2013 onwards, with a focus on ones from the past few years, finding that, globally, companies founded by women receive only about 2% of total venture-capital investments.

Female entrepreneurs are about 63% less likely to secure venture-capital funding than are men, and on average get only 70% of the amount that male entrepreneurs receive. This means that they are less likely to seek loans or investment in the first place, the report warns. One estimate in the report speculates that UK gross domestic product could have been 12% larger than it was in 2017 if women had started and scaled up businesses at the same rate as men did.

How I honed my biopharma dealmaking and business-development skills after my PhD

A second report on venture-capital allocation published last year paints a similar picture. It found that of the US$289 billion invested globally in 2024, 2.3% went to female-only founding teams, compared with 83.6% to all-male teams. Mixed-gender teams landed a 14.1% share of the funding pot.

The report, which was published by the London-based entrepreneur-support community the Founders Forum Group, also revealed that during fundraising women are more than twice as likely as male founders to be asked questions focused on risks. They are also interrupted almost five times more frequently than men are during pitch presentations and spend an average of 7.4 months fundraising compared with 5.2 months for their male counterparts.

The findings from these two reports will resonate with many female science entrepreneurs and those who support them. Four women tell Nature about their experiences learning to navigate a funding landscape in an ecosystem that can often seem hostile.

Worst critics

“Most of my investor conversations have been constructive and professional,” says Emma Yates, chief scientific officer at Proteotype Diagnostics in Cambridge, UK. She co-founded the company with her husband, its chief executive and chairperson, in 2019. “There have been isolated moments where I felt assumptions were being made that a male founder might not have faced, and a few investors were also uncomfortable with a husband-and-wife founding team,” Yates adds.

The company’s mission is to create an affordable early-cancer detection method based on the body’s immune response. So far, the firm has raised around $6.89 million in private and grant funding and the test is currently in a clinical trial, the final results of which are due at the end of the year. After that, Yates expects that they will start to seek series A funding — the first substantial round of start-up venture-capital financing — to take the company forwards.

In Yates’s view, female founders are often their own worst critics, which can make them less likely to seek funding for a good idea before they have a huge amount of evidence to back it up. “In science, you are trained to be cautious and to let the evidence speak,” she says. “Fundraising also requires you to communicate the scale of the opportunity before every uncertainty is removed. That was a learning curve for me.”

Ultimately, Yates thinks that “the bigger question now is whether women founders receive the same benefit of the doubt and access to growth capital”.

Careers advice from scientists in industry

Last year she received a £75,000 ( US$101,000) Women and Innovation Award from Innovate UK, the country’s national innovation agency, which Yates used to complete manufacturing validation of Proteotype’s diagnostic kit.

Business-development help came from other programmes. “The most useful support was very specific,” says Yates. It was crucial for “helping us think through clinical-study design, the technical evidence base, investor communication, commercial development and how to build the right plan around the science”.

In 2022, Yates had her first child. “Typically at that point in time, you’re wanting something with lots of job security so you can take a nice one-year maternity leave,” she says of the standard parental-leave practice in the United Kingdom. At the time, Proteotype still depended heavily on the founding team. “I was back on video calls within five weeks,” she says. “For founders, especially in science-based companies, the choice is often not a clean binary between being fully off or fully back at work.”

Yates would like to see innovation grants and founder-support programmes that provide temporary operational cover and childcare during parental leave. “For an early-stage science company, that kind of support could be the difference between maintaining momentum and a founder feeling they have to come back before they are ready,” she says.

Making the jump from a research career to founding her own company has been life changing for Yates. “I’m a different person than I was when I started,” she says. “I know how to lead a team, work with investors and clinical stakeholders, and make decisions under uncertainty. That is what science-based entrepreneurship requires.”

Perfectionism

Henriette Maaß, co-founder and chief executive of NanoStruct in Würzburg, Germany, credits the company’s foundation to a transfer grant from Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy. The company uses gold nanostructures to detect small quantities of contaminants, such as bacteria in the food industry. The grant enabled her to leave a project-management role at a semiconductor firm in 2021 and return to The Julius Maximilians University of Würzburg (where she completed her physics PhD two years earlier). There, she worked with Enno Schatz, a former colleague who would become chief technology officer at NanoStruct, to develop the idea that led to her co-founding the company.

More grants, including a €75,000 ($86,000) award from the European Union’s Women TechEU programme — which supports start-ups founded or co-founded by women who hold a top management position and own at least 25% of company shares — enabled the company to keep going. It now has ten employees and is looking for funding to take its product to market.

Henriette Maaß, co-founder and chief executive of NanoStruct, used government and European Union funding to launch and sustain her company.Credit: Enno Schatz

Maaß was pregnant when she started seeking early ‘seed’ funding for NanoStruct in 2025, and worried about how both potential funders and colleagues would react. “This was actually something I felt a bit insecure about but I knew I wanted to stay as chief executive of my company,” she says. She began to see the positive side of at least knowing they would attract investors who would be comfortable with a chief executive who is also a new mother.

Now, Maaß often takes her baby to meetings. “There is no one-fits-all advice,” she says. “Find your own way to manage both roles and don’t expect yourself to be perfect.”

Transitions

A key challenge faced by Kitiya Vongkamjan, chief executive at Unique Phage-Based Solutions (UniFAHS), was how to quickly turn herself from an academic into a businesswoman. She co-founded the Bangkok-based biotechnology company — which uses phage technology to target major food-borne pathogens — in 2020 with Chalita Wongpukdee, who is now the company’s chief marketing officer.

“We need to go from researchers to founders, and the ecosystem is so different” between the two sectors, says Vongkamjan. She thinks it takes courage for researchers to make that switch.

Vongkamjan received a Leaders in Innovation Fellowship from the UK Royal Academy of Engineering, which included a two-week entrepreneurship training course. At the end of the course, participants showcased their innovations in front of a panel of judges. Vongkamjan says that this taught her “all the skills for research to commercialization” and provided her with a mentor for the first two years of developing her spin-off. Financial help also came from the “three Fs”, Vongkamjan jokes — friends, family and fools — alongside commercialization support from start-up incubators at the Southern Regional Science Park at the Prince of Songkla University in Hay Yai, Thailand. Vongkamjan held an academic position there from 2012 to 2020. Her current institution, Kasetsart University in Bangkok, has also been supportive.

Meet the biotech-company founders driven by their child’s rare disease

In Asia, venture-capital funding often seems “out of reach” for women, says Vongkamjan, which might explain why her company didn’t progress as quickly as some of the companies that have a male founder, she adds. “People want to know, are you really a business person, or are you really just a research-focused person?”

Vongkamjan says that she has noticed women are also less likely to talk-up their successes. For example, she has been reticent to post about milestones reached by her business but says, “if you go on LinkedIn and you compare female and male founders, you see more posts” from the men. In 2025, a group of women even showed anecdotally, by posting with male aliases, that women’s LinkedIn posts tend to get less traffic than men’s do.

In 2024, UniFAHS completed a funding round of $1.4 million to move into other markets across southeast and South Asia. Funding came partly from ADB Ventures, an investment fund that Vongkamjan says has a reputation for supporting women. The company now employs 20 people but Vongkamjan has chosen to keep her food-microbiology laboratory at Kasetsart University, where she continues research that feeds into the company. She anticipates that will change as the company grows and everything will eventually be conducted in the company’s lab.

articles.personality_title: Women founders in science face funding gaps but find new support to grow
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Many women who want to start science-based businesses face big challenges. Studies show that women-led companies get only a tiny share of venture capital money compared to men, especially in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields.

**What happened**
Reports from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the Founders Forum Group reveal that female founders receive only about 2% of venture capital funding worldwide. Women also face more questions about risks and interruptions during fundraising. Four women leaders from science startups shared their stories about overcoming these challenges. For example, Emma Yates from the UK raised nearly $7 million for cancer detection tests but still sees bias and wants better support during parental leave. Henriette Maaß in Germany used government grants to start a company detecting food contaminants and manages work with motherhood. Kitiya Vongkamjan in Thailand turned her research into a business despite limited local funding for women, recently raising $1.4 million.

**Impact**
These stories show how hard it is for women to get funding and balance work with family in science startups. But targeted grants and support programs, like Innovate UK’s Women and Innovation Award and the EU’s Women TechEU, are helping women grow their businesses. This support helps female founders gain confidence, develop skills, and keep their companies moving forward, even when facing cultural and financial barriers.

**What's next step**
Experts and founders want more funding programs that offer money and practical help during times like parental leave. They also encourage women to share their successes more openly and build networks for business advice. As more women get support and funding, their companies can grow, creating new science innovations and stronger economies.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Though female science founders face funding gaps and bias, targeted support programs and personal determination are helping them build successful businesses and change the landscape.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les femmes fondatrices en science confrontées à un manque de financement mais soutenues pour grandir
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Beaucoup de femmes qui veulent créer des entreprises scientifiques font face à de grands obstacles. Les études montrent que les entreprises dirigées par des femmes reçoivent une très petite part des investissements en capital-risque comparé aux hommes, surtout dans les domaines des sciences, technologies, ingénierie et mathématiques (STEM).

**Ce qui s'est passé**
Des rapports de l'Organisation de coopération et de développement économiques (OCDE) et du Founders Forum Group révèlent que les femmes fondatrices reçoivent seulement environ 2 % du financement mondial en capital-risque. Les femmes sont aussi plus souvent questionnées sur les risques et interrompues lors des levées de fonds. Quatre dirigeantes de startups scientifiques ont partagé leurs expériences. Par exemple, Emma Yates au Royaume-Uni a levé près de 7 millions de dollars pour un test de détection du cancer, mais constate encore des biais et souhaite un meilleur soutien pendant le congé parental. Henriette Maaß en Allemagne a utilisé des subventions gouvernementales pour lancer une entreprise détectant des contaminants alimentaires, tout en conciliant travail et maternité. Kitiya Vongkamjan en Thaïlande a transformé sa recherche en entreprise malgré un financement local limité pour les femmes, levant récemment 1,4 million de dollars.

**Impact**
Ces récits montrent la difficulté pour les femmes d’obtenir des financements et de concilier travail et famille dans les startups scientifiques. Mais des programmes ciblés, comme le Women and Innovation Award d’Innovate UK et Women TechEU de l’UE, aident les femmes à développer leurs entreprises. Ce soutien renforce la confiance, les compétences et la progression des entreprises, malgré les barrières culturelles et financières.

**Prochaine étape**
Les experts et fondatrices souhaitent davantage de programmes offrant financement et aide pratique, notamment pendant le congé parental. Ils encouragent aussi les femmes à partager davantage leurs succès et à créer des réseaux d’entraide. Avec plus de soutien et de financement, ces entreprises pourront croître, apportant des innovations scientifiques et une économie plus forte.

**Résumé en une phrase**
Bien que les femmes fondatrices en science rencontrent des difficultés de financement et des biais, les programmes d’aide ciblés et leur détermination personnelle les aident à bâtir des entreprises prospères et à transformer le secteur.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres fundadoras en ciencia enfrentan brechas de financiamiento pero encuentran apoyo para crecer
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Muchas mujeres que quieren crear empresas basadas en la ciencia enfrentan grandes desafíos. Los estudios muestran que las empresas dirigidas por mujeres reciben solo una pequeña parte del capital de riesgo en comparación con los hombres, especialmente en ciencia, tecnología, ingeniería y matemáticas (STEM).

**Qué pasó**
Informes de la Organización para la Cooperación y el Desarrollo Económicos (OCDE) y del Founders Forum Group muestran que las fundadoras reciben solo alrededor del 2 % del financiamiento global de capital de riesgo. Además, las mujeres enfrentan más preguntas sobre riesgos y son interrumpidas con más frecuencia durante la recaudación de fondos. Cuatro mujeres líderes de startups científicas compartieron sus historias. Por ejemplo, Emma Yates del Reino Unido recaudó casi 7 millones de dólares para pruebas de detección temprana de cáncer, pero aún nota prejuicios y desea mejor apoyo durante la licencia parental. Henriette Maaß en Alemania usó subvenciones gubernamentales para iniciar una empresa que detecta contaminantes en alimentos, combinando trabajo y maternidad. Kitiya Vongkamjan en Tailandia convirtió su investigación en negocio a pesar del financiamiento limitado para mujeres localmente, y recientemente recaudó 1.4 millones de dólares.

**Impacto**
Estas historias muestran lo difícil que es para las mujeres obtener financiamiento y equilibrar trabajo y familia en startups científicas. Pero programas de apoyo específicos, como el Women and Innovation Award de Innovate UK y Women TechEU de la UE, están ayudando a las mujeres a crecer sus negocios. Este apoyo les da confianza, habilidades y mantiene sus empresas avanzando, a pesar de las barreras culturales y financieras.

**Próximo paso**
Expertos y fundadoras quieren más programas que ofrezcan dinero y ayuda práctica durante momentos como la licencia parental. También animan a las mujeres a compartir sus éxitos y crear redes de apoyo. Con más apoyo y financiamiento, estas empresas podrán crecer, generando nuevas innovaciones científicas y economías más fuertes.

**Resumen en una frase**
Aunque las fundadoras mujeres enfrentan brechas de financiamiento y prejuicios, los programas de apoyo dirigidos y su determinación las están ayudando a construir negocios exitosos y cambiar el panorama.

articles.title: Chadian environmental activist Hindou Oumarou: ‘AI governance must respect Indigenous peoples’
articles.summary: How AI expansion may affect environments, water and biodiversity, or the rights of communities whose territories and knowledge are being encroached upon
articles.content:
This article by Brian Obara was originally published by Dialogue Earth on August 13, 2026. It is republished on Global Voices as part of a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Dialogue Earth speaks with the Chadian environmental activist Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim about Indigenous perspectives on AI.

As African governments develop national artificial intelligence strategies, questions of safety, economic competition and employment have dominated the policy debate.

Less attention has been paid to how AI expansion may affect environments, water and biodiversity, or the rights of communities whose territories and knowledge are being encroached upon.

These concerns arise at several points in the AI value chain. The associated data centres require energy, water and land, while their hardware depends on mineral supply chains.

AI systems may collect and reproduce cultural, linguistic and environmental knowledge without recognising that such information is often held collectively by a community, rather than by an individual. This is important because conventional data protection frameworks tend to focus on individual data privacy and ownership, making them poorly equipped to protect collectively held information.

In July, the UN held its first-ever Global Dialogue on AI Governance, in Geneva, Switzerland. Among those in attendance was Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim. She is president of the Association for Indigenous Women and Peoples of Chad, and a former chair of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. While there, she took part in discussions on advancing environmentally sustainable AI governance that also respects the rights of Indigenous peoples.

Here, Ibrahim tells Dialogue Earth about the importance of bringing Indigenous perspectives to Africa’s AI governance debate. She explains why African governments should incorporate biodiversity, land rights and collectively owned data considerations into their AI policies. She says Indigenous peoples must be recognised as rights holders and decision-makers – especially when newfangled technology has implications for their lands or intellectual heritage.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Dialogue Earth: As African countries develop national AI strategies, what opportunities do governments have to reflect the continent’s environmental realities and cultural diversity?

Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim: Africa is home to extraordinary biological and cultural diversity, but it also faces significant pressures from climate change, mineral extraction, land degradation and infrastructure expansion. National AI strategies should therefore connect technological development with biodiversity protection, climate resilience, land rights and the responsible management of natural resources.

African governments can lead by requiring environmental and social impact assessments for AI infrastructure. This would help protect water and land from unsustainable data centre development, and ensure that mineral demand does not drive ecosystem destruction or dispossession.

They can also make Indigenous peoples formal participants in AI governance and protect collective rights over our rich and diverse cultural, linguistic and environmental data.

There is also an opportunity to invest in African and community-controlled AI capacity: local research institutions, Indigenous peoples’ innovation centres, African language and culture models, and technologies designed for African and community needs, rather than external markets.

What are current AI governance debates missing by leaving biodiversity and Indigenous rights at the margins?

AI governance has largely been built around a western, human-centred understanding of risk. Policymakers are rightly concerned about issues such as misinformation, employment, discrimination and security. But they have paid far less attention to the natural systems that make economies and societies possible. As a result, biodiversity loss, ecosystem damage and Indigenous peoples’ rights are rarely treated as core AI governance issues.

There is also a wider risk. Without ecological guardrails, AI could accelerate extraction, consumption and infrastructure development in ways that place even greater pressure on ecosystems and Indigenous peoples. Many of the lands under pressure from the mineral, energy and infrastructure sectors are Indigenous peoples’ territories and biodiversity-rich areas.

AI governance cannot be described as responsible if it does not protect the ecosystems and cultures on which communities depend.

What should meaningful Indigenous participation in AI governance involve?

Indigenous peoples should help shape the safeguards that protect their rights, knowledge and territories. They should participate in decisions about how systems affecting them are deployed. This must be done with respect for free, prior and informed consent.

Participation is not only about consultation. Indigenous peoples must be recognised as decision-makers and rights holders, particularly when AI policies, infrastructure projects or data practices affect their land, knowledge or cultural heritage.

How are existing data protection systems failing to protect knowledge and data held collectively by communities, rather than individuals?

Conventional data protection systems tend to focus on individual privacy. They do not adequately protect a community’s collective rights over its language, cultural heritage, traditional knowledge or territorial information.

Indigenous peoples must retain control over whether and how their knowledge and data are used. Governments and companies should recognise that Indigenous peoples’ data is often collective and develop consultation frameworks that reflect this.

AI companies should also audit their models for linguistic and cultural bias, include Indigenous leaders and experts throughout the process, and create mechanisms that allow communities to challenge or remove inaccurate or harmful representations.

Can AI support Indigenous knowledge and conservation without replacing community expertise?

There are encouraging examples in which AI is supporting, rather than replacing, Indigenous peoples’ knowledge. Some examples are outlined in a recent report to the UN Economic and Social Council on Indigenous peoples and AI.

In the Amazon, Indigenous communities have worked with NGOs and researchers to use AI-supported satellite monitoring to detect illegal deforestation and mining. In Chad, participatory mapping and predictive analysis have been combined with pastoral knowledge to anticipate drought and protect herder’s migration routes. In the Arctic, Sámi and Inuit communities have integrated traditional knowledge with predictive models to monitor changes in sea ice, wildlife movements and the impacts of extractive industries.

The important point is that the technology should strengthen existing knowledge rather than replace it. Indigenous peoples bring detailed, place-based understanding accumulated over generations. AI can help analyse information and identify patterns, but it cannot substitute for the cultural context, relationships and judgement that make that knowledge meaningful.

AI can also help communities and conservation organisations process large volumes of information more quickly. It can support the detection of deforestation and illegal extraction, identify changes in ecosystems, analyse satellite or acoustic data, predict environmental threats and improve monitoring in places that have historically lacked resources.

The strongest opportunities are those in which AI supports priorities defined by communities themselves and strengthens the capacity of people already protecting nature.

But these benefits are not automatic. Technology can reinforce inequality when tools are designed without community participation, when data is extracted without consent, or when communities lack the infrastructure and funding needed to use the systems themselves.

Using AI to monitor forest loss does not compensate for an AI growth model that drives greater energy use, mineral extraction, water consumption or habitat destruction.

What is one AI governance recommendation you would make to world leaders?

Leaders must ensure that no AI system, policy or infrastructure project affecting Indigenous peoples, their data or their territories proceeds without their free, prior and informed consent. That principle should apply across the entire AI value chain: from the extraction of minerals and construction of data centres to the collection of Indigenous peoples’ knowledge, and the deployment of AI tools in communities.

This is not only about preventing harm. It is about recognising Indigenous peoples as decision-makers and rights holders. World leaders should embed Indigenous peoples’ participation and data sovereignty directly into national and international AI governance frameworks, rather than treating them as optional social safeguards.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant and positive development in AI governance by advocating for the inclusion and respect of Indigenous peoples' rights and environmental concerns. It addresses broad societal and environmental impacts of AI, emphasizing Indigenous participation and data sovereignty, which has meaningful implications for policy and global governance frameworks.
articles.personality_title: Chadian activist calls for Indigenous rights in AI governance
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As artificial intelligence (AI) grows rapidly in Africa, governments are creating new rules and plans to manage it. While most focus on jobs, safety, and competition, important issues like protecting nature and Indigenous peoples’ rights receive less attention.

**What happened** – Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, a Chadian environmental activist and Indigenous leader, spoke at the United Nations’ first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026. She urged African governments to include Indigenous voices in decisions about AI. She highlighted how AI systems affect land, water, biodiversity, and the knowledge held by Indigenous communities.

**Impact** – Ibrahim’s message is important because AI activities—like building data centers or using Indigenous knowledge—can harm ecosystems and communities if not carefully managed. Current rules mostly protect individuals, not groups or communities, which means Indigenous cultural and environmental knowledge can be used without permission. By involving Indigenous peoples as decision-makers, AI policies can better protect the environment and respect collective rights.

**What's next step** – African governments are encouraged to require environmental checks before AI projects begin and recognize Indigenous peoples’ rights to their land and knowledge. Supporting local research and technologies that meet community needs can help balance AI growth with nature and culture. The goal is to build AI systems that support Indigenous knowledge rather than replace it.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Including Indigenous peoples in AI governance ensures technology respects their rights and protects the environment in Africa’s growing AI landscape.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une activiste tchadienne plaide pour les droits des peuples autochtones dans la gouvernance de l’IA
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Alors que l’intelligence artificielle (IA) se développe rapidement en Afrique, les gouvernements créent de nouvelles règles pour la gérer. La plupart se concentrent sur l’emploi, la sécurité et la concurrence, mais la protection de la nature et des droits des peuples autochtones est souvent négligée.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, militante environnementale tchadienne et leader autochtone, a pris la parole lors du premier Dialogue mondial sur la gouvernance de l’IA aux Nations Unies en juillet 2026. Elle a appelé les gouvernements africains à inclure les voix autochtones dans les décisions liées à l’IA, soulignant l’impact des systèmes d’IA sur les terres, l’eau, la biodiversité et les savoirs autochtones.

**Impact** – Le message d’Ibrahim est important car les activités liées à l’IA—comme la construction de centres de données ou l’utilisation des savoirs autochtones—peuvent nuire aux écosystèmes et aux communautés si elles ne sont pas bien encadrées. Les règles actuelles protègent surtout les individus, pas les groupes, ce qui permet d’utiliser les savoirs collectifs sans consentement. Impliquer les peuples autochtones comme décideurs permettrait de mieux protéger l’environnement et leurs droits collectifs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les gouvernements africains sont encouragés à exiger des évaluations environnementales avant tout projet d’IA et à reconnaître les droits des peuples autochtones sur leurs terres et leurs savoirs. Soutenir la recherche locale et les technologies adaptées aux besoins des communautés aidera à concilier développement de l’IA, nature et culture. L’objectif est de créer des systèmes d’IA qui renforcent les savoirs autochtones plutôt que de les remplacer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Inclure les peuples autochtones dans la gouvernance de l’IA garantit que la technologie respecte leurs droits et protège l’environnement dans le développement de l’IA en Afrique.
articles.personality_title_es: Activista chadiana pide respeto a derechos indígenas en la gobernanza de la IA
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Con el rápido crecimiento de la inteligencia artificial (IA) en África, los gobiernos están creando nuevas reglas para manejarla. La mayoría se enfoca en empleos, seguridad y competencia, pero temas importantes como la protección del medio ambiente y los derechos indígenas reciben menos atención.

**Qué pasó** – Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, activista ambiental de Chad y líder indígena, habló en el primer Diálogo Global sobre Gobernanza de la IA en las Naciones Unidas en julio de 2026. Pidió a los gobiernos africanos incluir las voces indígenas en las decisiones sobre la IA, destacando cómo los sistemas de IA afectan las tierras, el agua, la biodiversidad y los conocimientos indígenas.

**Impacto** – El mensaje de Ibrahim es importante porque las actividades relacionadas con la IA—como construir centros de datos o usar conocimientos indígenas—pueden dañar ecosistemas y comunidades si no se gestionan bien. Las reglas actuales protegen principalmente a individuos, no a grupos, lo que permite usar conocimientos colectivos sin permiso. Incluir a los pueblos indígenas como tomadores de decisiones puede proteger mejor el medio ambiente y sus derechos colectivos.

**Próximo paso** – Se anima a los gobiernos africanos a exigir evaluaciones ambientales antes de proyectos de IA y a reconocer los derechos indígenas sobre sus tierras y conocimientos. Apoyar la investigación local y tecnologías adaptadas a las necesidades comunitarias ayudará a equilibrar el crecimiento de la IA con la naturaleza y cultura. El objetivo es crear sistemas de IA que apoyen los conocimientos indígenas, no que los reemplacen.

**Resumen en una frase** – Incluir a los pueblos indígenas en la gobernanza de la IA asegura que la tecnología respete sus derechos y proteja el medio ambiente en el desarrollo de la IA en África.

articles.title: DNA reveals a society organised around women in pre-Roman Britain
articles.summary: Descent passed from mother to daughter rather than from father to son, a study of more than 500 Iron Age individuals from north-east England suggests
articles.content:
Descent passed from mother to daughter rather than from father to son, a study of more than 500 Iron Age individuals from north-east England suggests

Boudica was a powerful ancient Briton who led a rebellion against the Romans Science History Images/Alamy

The DNA of more than 500 individuals who were buried in the north-east of England over a period of several centuries before the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43 has been sequenced. It reveals a society organised around women, with large clans for which descent could be traced down the female line for up to nine generations, but where fathers were often absent from burial sites.

The study also reveals that some women had multiple male partners and shows a pattern of repeated unions between two maternal clans. “It’s revolutionary, and will totally change the way we think about the Iron Age,” says Rachel Pope at the University of Liverpool in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the study.

It was suggested in the 1860s that early societies were female-led, but the idea was rejected by later anthropologists, who assumed male-led societies were the natural order. From the 1950s onwards, however, discoveries in Europe of lavish burials of ancient women showed that in some societies women could be of high status at the very least.

Advertisement

More recently, studies of ancient DNA have begun adding to the evidence. Last year a study of around 50 individuals buried in south-west England revealed that women remained in their ancestral homes while men moved around, a pattern known as matrilocality.

Now Ian Armit at the University of York, UK, and his colleagues have sequenced the DNA of around 500 individuals associated with the Arras culture, famed for its chariot burials. The remains of nearly 400 of these individuals were excavated by other archaeological teams at Wetwang Slack in the East Riding of Yorkshire, which was most active between the fourth and second centuries BC and is the largest known Iron Age burial ground in Britain. The rest came from nearby sites.

The Arras DNA also reveals a strong matrilocal pattern. Most of the women buried at Wetwang Slack also had close relatives buried there, such as a mother, for instance, but this was rarer for men. In a few cases, the team found direct evidence that a man originating from one site fathered children at another – in other words, that men moved around while women stayed put.

Matrilocality by itself doesn’t necessarily mean that women ruled a society. But it is generally associated with higher status and better conditions for women. An individual who leaves home to live with the family of a partner is reliant on that family and thus is in a weaker position than one who stays.

However, when the DNA evidence is combined with other evidence, it does point to societies where women could rule. “For Britain, the archaeological evidence supports a more equitable Iron Age than scholars had previously imagined, and some powerful women were certainly part of that,” says Pope. “From [bone injuries], we can even see now that some women were in combat with Rome.”

“Powerful Iron Age women abound in the texts: Onomaris, Boudica, Cartimandua, Celts with their women as judges,” she says. “Historians of the 1860s and 1870s believed in a largely matriarchal Iron Age until 1880s English anthropology asserted a patriarchal norm.”

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

That said, there was also regional diversity in how societies were organised, says Pope. Other DNA studies suggest that Iron Age societies in south-east England, for instance, weren’t matrilocal.

At least 12 of the Arras women had children with more than one man. This could reflect serial monogamy, the team members – who declined to be interviewed for this story – write in a preprint, but it could also reflect “polyandrous reproductive arrangements within a strongly female-line-centred social structure”. In other words, women could have had multiple husbands simultaneously, as some Roman sources claim was the case.

The team did find one case where a man had children with a woman and with her daughter, but this was exceptional.

The genetics also show that individuals from the same maternal lineage avoided having children with each other. Because these people lived in small groups in which a large proportion of people were related, this must have been deliberate and based on knowledge of people’s ancestry. “[T]his avoidance demonstrates detailed knowledge of maternal-line affiliation across many generations and possibly hundreds of years,” the study concludes.

The exceptions to this were the three individuals – two male, one female – buried with chariots. “The individuals afforded chariot burials at Wetwang Slack stood apart by showing recurrent close kin unions, consistent with a reproductive strategy in which high status, identity and claims to particular forms of burial were concentrated within a restricted descent group,” the study says.

All these lines of evidence point to a society organised around women rather than men, the researchers conclude. “[F]emale-line descent was not an incidental feature of Arras culture communities, but a central organising principle, as it may well have been across the communities of Iron Age Britain more broadly.”

“It is an excellent paper, closely argued and very rich in data and inference,” says Daniel Bradley at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, who was part of the team that studied the 50 or so individuals buried in south-west England.

“We did notice a tendency for marriage across [maternal lineages] in our study, but the finding here of a sustained pattern of unions between two different maternal clan groups is really striking. It implies a deep knowledge of family histories – of which maternal social axis one belonged to – and perhaps of an alliance forming between them,” Bradley says.
articles.reasoning: The article reveals groundbreaking scientific evidence that challenges long-held assumptions about gender roles in ancient societies, showing that pre-Roman Iron Age Britain had a female-centered social structure. This discovery promotes a more equitable understanding of history, highlighting women's leadership and social status, which can inspire contemporary discussions on gender equality and human rights.
articles.personality_title: DNA reveals women-led society in ancient Iron Age Britain
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists studied the DNA of more than 500 people buried in northeast England before the Roman invasion in AD 43. These remains come from the Iron Age, a period long before written history in Britain.

**What happened** – Researchers found that families were traced through mothers rather than fathers. Women stayed in their home communities, while men often moved between groups. Some women had children with more than one man. The study focused on the Arras culture, known for its special chariot burials, and showed that women’s family lines were central to society.

**Impact** – This discovery changes how we understand ancient British societies. It shows that women had important social roles and could have been leaders. Unlike past beliefs that men always ruled, this evidence shows a society where women’s family ties and status mattered most for many generations.

**What's next step** – Scientists will compare these findings with other regions of Iron Age Britain to see how common this female-centered society was. This research may also inspire new studies about women’s roles in other ancient cultures.

**One-sentence takeaway** – DNA evidence reveals that pre-Roman Iron Age Britain was organized around women, with families traced through mothers and women playing key social roles.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ADN révèle une société dirigée par les femmes dans la Grande-Bretagne de l’âge du fer
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des scientifiques ont étudié l’ADN de plus de 500 personnes enterrées dans le nord-est de l’Angleterre avant l’invasion romaine en 43 après J.-C. Ces restes datent de l’âge du fer, une période bien avant l’histoire écrite en Grande-Bretagne.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les chercheurs ont découvert que les familles étaient tracées par les mères plutôt que par les pères. Les femmes restaient dans leur communauté d’origine, tandis que les hommes bougeaient souvent entre les groupes. Certaines femmes avaient des enfants avec plusieurs hommes. L’étude a porté sur la culture d’Arras, connue pour ses tombes de chars, et a montré que les lignées maternelles étaient centrales dans la société.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change notre compréhension des sociétés anciennes britanniques. Elle montre que les femmes avaient des rôles sociaux importants et pouvaient être des leaders. Contrairement aux croyances passées où les hommes dominaient toujours, cette preuve montre une société où la famille et le statut des femmes comptaient sur plusieurs générations.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont comparer ces résultats avec d’autres régions de la Grande-Bretagne à l’âge du fer pour voir à quel point cette société centrée sur les femmes était courante. Cette recherche pourrait aussi inspirer de nouvelles études sur le rôle des femmes dans d’autres cultures anciennes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’ADN révèle que la Grande-Bretagne pré-romaine de l’âge du fer était organisée autour des femmes, avec des familles suivies par la mère et des femmes jouant des rôles sociaux clés.
articles.personality_title_es: El ADN revela una sociedad dirigida por mujeres en la Gran Bretaña de la Edad de Hierro
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Científicos estudiaron el ADN de más de 500 personas enterradas en el noreste de Inglaterra antes de la invasión romana en el año 43 d.C. Estos restos son de la Edad de Hierro, mucho antes de la historia escrita en Gran Bretaña.

**Qué pasó** – Los investigadores encontraron que las familias se rastreaban por las madres en lugar de por los padres. Las mujeres permanecían en sus comunidades, mientras que los hombres se movían entre grupos. Algunas mujeres tuvieron hijos con varios hombres. El estudio se centró en la cultura Arras, conocida por sus enterramientos con carros, y mostró que las líneas familiares maternas eran centrales en la sociedad.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento cambia la forma en que entendemos las sociedades antiguas británicas. Muestra que las mujeres tenían roles sociales importantes y podían ser líderes. Contrario a creencias anteriores donde los hombres dominaban, esta evidencia muestra una sociedad donde las familias y el estatus de las mujeres importaban por muchas generaciones.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos compararán estos hallazgos con otras regiones de la Edad de Hierro en Gran Bretaña para ver qué tan común era esta sociedad centrada en mujeres. Esta investigación también podría inspirar nuevos estudios sobre el papel de las mujeres en otras culturas antiguas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La evidencia del ADN revela que la Gran Bretaña pre-romana de la Edad de Hierro estaba organizada alrededor de las mujeres, con familias rastreadas por la madre y mujeres con roles sociales clave.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Afghanistan education, Myanmar flooding, Syria recovery, homecare workers in New York
articles.summary: Five years since the Taliban seized power in Kabul, life for some Afghans has improved while many others suffer growing hardship.
articles.content:
Although many families in rural Afghanistan struggle to secure food and water, the UN’s aid coordination office spokesperson Olga Cherevko said on Thursday that the chief concern is the continuing ban on girls’ education.

Tweet URL

“They told me that basically they had lost hope for their daughter’s future and of course for themselves,” Ms. Cherevko told UN News. “That really stayed with me because this is also a community struggling simply to make ends meet and to survive.”

The senior humanitarian told UN News that Afghan women today have fewer opportunities to earn income than men, because of increasing restrictions placed on them by the de facto authorities.

As a result, women are finding it harder to support their families, while also having to cope with reduced opportunities to participate in life outside their homes, Ms. Cherevko said.

Obstacles to stability remain

In an assessment of the situation in Afghanistan on Thursday, the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said that the past five years of Taliban rule had brought a reduction in conflict and “tangible benefits” for some.

But significant obstacles to lasting stability remain, particularly the “increasingly damaging restrictions” on women and girls and ongoing terrorism concerns.

“The last five years have shown that Afghans deeply value peace and stability after decades of war,” said UNAMA Officer-in-Charge Georgette Gagnon.

“Afghanistan’s future depends on building a society in which the rights and potential of all Afghans are realised and institutions are responsive and accountable,” she added.

Myanmar floods threaten to deepen hunger crisis: WFP

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has launched an emergency response operation in Myanmar, where monsoon flooding threatens to push vulnerable communities deeper into hunger.

The agency has begun distributing fortified biscuits in Laymyethna Township, Ayeyarwady region in southwestern Myanmar.

Flooding caused by heavy rainfall there over the last two weeks has breached river embankments and inundated villages.

WFP rapid assessments have indicated that more than 32,000 people across nearly 100 villages have been affected.

Food assistance on the way

The 20 tons of fortified biscuits already dispatched to UN partners will provide immediate food assistance to 10,000 people.

“Flooding is a recurring threat, but this year it is impacting communities already battered by multiple underlying crises,” said WFP Representative Michael Dunford.

The emergency represents a new challenge for Myanmar’s people. An estimated 12.4 million people are already going hungry amid an ongoing civil war, displacement, economic hardship and high food prices.

WFP has appealed for urgent funding and sustained aid access to prevent the crisis from worsening.

Tweet URL

UN urges global solidarity as Syria recovery reaches ‘historic turning point’

A growing number of people displaced by the Syrian conflict are returning home, creating a critical juncture for the country’s recovery, according to the head of the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) Barham Salih.

Well over a decade of conflict in Syria claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and led to one of the most serious global displacement crises of recent years.

Nearly four million Syrian refugees remain in Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq and Egypt, and 5.5 million people are still displaced inside Syria.

“Syria is at a historic turning point,” said Mr. Salih. “More than three million Syrians have already returned from abroad or inside the country since December 2024, demonstrating their determination to rebuild.”

He added that “recovery on this scale is a huge task, and Syria cannot do it alone. The international community must step in, and swiftly. Without this, a historic opportunity to help the country rebuild and to stabilise the region will be missed.”

The Syrian Government wants a sustainable recovery, and is advocating a “No Tents, No Camps” vision.

UN on the ground

UNHCR is already collaborating closely with Syrian authorities and other development partners to address recovery needs.

It is providing shelter rehabilitation, restoration of basic services, legal and civil documentation, housing, land and property assistance, livelihoods programmes and cash assistance.

“Syrians are determined to rebuild,” Mr. Salih said. “The international community must match that determination with sustained support.”

Human rights experts condemn treatment of NY care workers

Independent UN human rights experts reiterated concerns on Thursday about what they describe as a Government-subsidised 24-hour workday system for homecare workers in New York City.

These care workers, who are predominantly migrant women, went on a hunger strike between late July and early August to protest having to work 24 hours a day while – in practice – being undercompensated under state law.

“We are seriously concerned that the reported system may enable exploitative practices and that it has a disproportionate impact on migrant women and their families,” the UN Human Rights Council-appointed investigators said.

Under New York State’s Medicaid-funded homecare system, employers must pay wages for 13 hours of a 24-hour shift, under the assumption that workers use the remaining 11 hours to eat and sleep.

Homecare system reflects inequalities

The experts noted that the concentration of migrant women in homecare “reflects the persistent undervaluation of care work and gendered inequalities in labour markets, which may expose women to heightened risks of exploitation and abuse.”

The situation for homecare workers in New York could even amount to forced labour under International Labour Organization (ILO) standards, according to the independent experts, who receive no salary for their work from any UN entity and are not employed by any organization.

Local and state authorities must work to improve conditions, ensure access to effective remedies and reform or eliminate the 24-hour workday system in line with international human rights standards, the experts said.

“Homecare workers must be able to enjoy just, favourable and safe working conditions, adequate rest, fair remuneration, protection of their rights, and access to effective remedies,” they said.

articles.personality_title: UN reports progress and challenges in Afghanistan, Myanmar, Syria, and New York care workers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations shared updates on four important global issues: Afghanistan’s ongoing struggles under Taliban rule, severe flooding in Myanmar, Syria’s recovery after years of war, and difficult working conditions for homecare workers in New York.

**What happened** – In Afghanistan, five years after the Taliban took control, many families face food and water shortages, and girls remain banned from school. The UN says women have fewer job chances and face more restrictions. In Myanmar, recent heavy rains caused floods that affected over 32,000 people, prompting the UN World Food Programme to send emergency food supplies to 10,000 people. Meanwhile, Syria is seeing a growing number of refugees returning home after more than a decade of conflict. The UN is helping rebuild homes and services but calls for more international support. In New York City, homecare workers, mostly migrant women, protested against a 24-hour work system that pays them for only part of their shifts. UN experts warn this system can lead to exploitation and call for better working conditions.

**Impact** – These stories show both challenges and progress. Afghanistan’s situation highlights the deep effects of restrictions on women and girls, affecting families’ futures. Myanmar’s floods add to existing hardships, but quick food aid helps prevent hunger. Syria’s return of millions of displaced people marks a hopeful step toward peace and rebuilding, but it needs global help to succeed. The concerns about New York’s homecare workers reveal how important fair work rules are to protect vulnerable workers and ensure their rights.

**What’s next step** – In Afghanistan, the UN and others continue to urge for girls’ education and women’s rights to improve. In Myanmar, the World Food Programme seeks more funding to reach more people affected by floods and ongoing crises. Syria’s recovery depends on stronger international support to rebuild infrastructure and services for returning families. In New York, human rights experts call on local and state governments to change the 24-hour work system to meet international labor standards and protect care workers.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN reports show ongoing efforts to support vulnerable people worldwide, from education and food aid to rebuilding communities and improving workers’ rights.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le rapport de l’ONU sur les progrès et défis en Afghanistan, Myanmar, Syrie et pour les aides à domicile à New York
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Nations Unies ont partagé des informations sur quatre enjeux mondiaux importants : les difficultés en Afghanistan sous le régime taliban, les inondations graves au Myanmar, la reconstruction en Syrie après des années de guerre, et les conditions de travail difficiles des aides à domicile à New York.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En Afghanistan, cinq ans après la prise de pouvoir des talibans, de nombreuses familles manquent de nourriture et d’eau, et les filles sont toujours interdites d’école. L’ONU indique que les femmes ont moins d’opportunités d’emploi et subissent plus de restrictions. Au Myanmar, de fortes pluies ont provoqué des inondations touchant plus de 32 000 personnes, ce qui a poussé le Programme alimentaire mondial à envoyer des vivres d’urgence à 10 000 personnes. En Syrie, un nombre croissant de réfugiés rentrent chez eux après plus de dix ans de conflit. L’ONU aide à reconstruire logements et services, mais demande plus de soutien international. À New York, des aides à domicile, principalement des femmes migrantes, ont protesté contre un système de travail de 24 heures payé partiellement. Des experts de l’ONU alertent sur les risques d’exploitation et demandent de meilleures conditions.

**Impact** – Ces histoires montrent à la fois des défis et des progrès. La situation en Afghanistan souligne les effets profonds des restrictions sur les femmes et les filles, qui touchent les familles. Les inondations au Myanmar aggravent les difficultés existantes, mais l’aide alimentaire rapide aide à prévenir la faim. Le retour de millions de Syriens marque une étape encourageante vers la paix et la reconstruction, mais a besoin d’un soutien mondial. Les préoccupations sur les aides à domicile à New York montrent l’importance de règles du travail justes pour protéger les travailleurs vulnérables.

**Prochaines étapes** – En Afghanistan, l’ONU et d’autres continuent de demander l’accès à l’éducation pour les filles et le respect des droits des femmes. Au Myanmar, le Programme alimentaire mondial cherche plus de fonds pour aider davantage de personnes touchées par les inondations et les crises. La reconstruction syrienne dépend d’un soutien international renforcé pour rétablir les infrastructures et services. À New York, les experts des droits humains appellent les autorités à modifier le système de travail de 24 heures pour respecter les normes internationales et protéger les aides à domicile.

**Phrase clé** – Le rapport de l’ONU montre des efforts continus pour soutenir les personnes vulnérables dans le monde, de l’éducation et l’aide alimentaire à la reconstruction et à la défense des droits des travailleurs.
articles.personality_title_es: Informe de la ONU sobre avances y retos en Afganistán, Myanmar, Siria y trabajadores de cuidado en Nueva York
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las Naciones Unidas compartieron noticias sobre cuatro temas globales importantes: las dificultades en Afganistán bajo el control talibán, las graves inundaciones en Myanmar, la recuperación en Siria tras años de guerra y las difíciles condiciones laborales de los trabajadores de cuidado en Nueva York.

**Qué pasó** – En Afganistán, cinco años después de que los talibanes tomaran el poder, muchas familias sufren falta de comida y agua, y las niñas siguen sin poder ir a la escuela. La ONU dice que las mujeres tienen menos oportunidades de trabajo y enfrentan más restricciones. En Myanmar, fuertes lluvias causaron inundaciones que afectaron a más de 32,000 personas, por lo que el Programa Mundial de Alimentos envió ayuda alimentaria de emergencia para 10,000 personas. En Siria, un número creciente de refugiados regresa a casa después de más de una década de conflicto. La ONU ayuda a reconstruir viviendas y servicios, pero pide más apoyo internacional. En Nueva York, trabajadores de cuidado, en su mayoría mujeres migrantes, protestaron contra un sistema de trabajo de 24 horas que solo les paga por parte de su turno. Expertos de la ONU advierten sobre riesgos de explotación y piden mejores condiciones laborales.

**Impacto** – Estas historias muestran tanto desafíos como avances. La situación en Afganistán resalta los efectos profundos de las restricciones a mujeres y niñas, que afectan a las familias. Las inundaciones en Myanmar empeoran las dificultades existentes, pero la ayuda rápida previene el hambre. El regreso de millones en Siria es un paso esperanzador hacia la paz y la reconstrucción, pero necesita ayuda global. Las preocupaciones sobre los trabajadores de cuidado en Nueva York muestran la importancia de reglas laborales justas para proteger a los trabajadores vulnerables.

**Próximo paso** – En Afganistán, la ONU y otros siguen pidiendo educación para niñas y derechos para mujeres. En Myanmar, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos busca más fondos para ayudar a más personas afectadas por las inundaciones y crisis. La recuperación de Siria depende de mayor apoyo internacional para restaurar infraestructura y servicios. En Nueva York, expertos en derechos humanos llaman a los gobiernos a cambiar el sistema de trabajo de 24 horas para cumplir con estándares internacionales y proteger a los trabajadores.

**Frase clave** – El informe de la ONU muestra esfuerzos continuos para apoyar a las personas vulnerables en todo el mundo, desde educación y ayuda alimentaria hasta reconstrucción y defensa de los derechos laborales.
